units.title: Unit 85 — The senses
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 85. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
learningObjectives: Name the five senses and identify the associated perception verbs.
Use look, sound, taste, smell and feel with adjectives to report impressions.
Describe comparisons with like + noun and impressions with as if/as though + clause.
Use seem and appear to express impressions and choose natural complements.
Distinguish seeing from looking and watching, hearing from listening, and feeling from touching.
Use the nouns look, sound, smell and taste to discuss impressions and preferences.

items.example: Good lighting is important for people with poor sight.
items.note: The sense that allows you to see.

items.example: Her hearing is excellent, even when the sound is quiet.
items.note: The sense that allows you to hear.

items.example: Our sense of taste helps us notice different flavours.
items.note: As a noun here, taste refers to one of the five senses.

items.example: Dogs have a very strong sense of smell.
items.note: As a noun here, smell means the ability to notice odours.

items.example: You can recognise some materials by touch.
items.note: As a noun here, touch is the physical sense of contact.

items.example: I can see the mountains from my window.
items.note: See describes visual perception, without necessarily looking deliberately.

items.example: I could hear a dog barking in the distance.
items.note: Hear describes receiving sound, not necessarily paying attention to it.

items.example: Taste the sauce before you add more salt.
items.note: As a verb, taste can mean test the flavour of food or drink.

items.example: I can smell fresh coffee from the kitchen.
items.note: As a verb, smell can mean notice an odour.

items.pt: sentir ao tocar; perceber pelo tato
items.example: I could feel the cold wind on my face.
items.note: Feel can describe a physical sensation or what you notice by touch.

items.example: You look tired after your long journey.
items.note: Look + adjective describes an impression based on appearance; no like before an adjective.

items.pt: parecer estrangeiro pelo sotaque ou som
items.example: That accent sounds foreign to me, but I cannot place it.
items.note: Sound + adjective reports an impression based on what you hear.

items.example: This tea tastes strange without sugar.
items.note: Taste + adjective describes the flavour of something.

items.example: The flowers smell wonderful after the rain.
items.note: Smell + adjective describes an odour.

items.example: The towels still feel damp, so leave them outside.
items.note: Feel + adjective describes the texture or physical condition of something.

items.example: The grass was damp after the morning rain.
items.note: Slightly wet, often when that is unpleasant or inconvenient.

items.example: I like the look of this little cafe.
items.note: Look is a noun here: the visible appearance of a person or thing.

items.example: I love the sound of rain on the roof.
items.note: Sound is a noun here, and of introduces the source of the sound.

items.example: I enjoy the smell of bread in the morning.
items.note: Use the smell of + noun to talk about a particular odour. Reinforced by the personalisation task.

items.example: I love the taste of fresh strawberries.
items.note: Taste as a noun can mean the flavour of a particular food. Reinforced by the personalisation task.

items.pt: parecer-se com alguém ou algo; ter aparência de
items.example: From a distance, the building looks like a castle.
items.note: Use look like + noun, not look like + adjective. With an adjective use look + adjective.

items.pt: soar como algo; parecer algo pelo som
items.example: The noise outside sounds like a motorbike.
items.note: Use sound like + noun for a comparison based on hearing.

items.pt: ter cheiro de algo; cheirar a
items.example: The soap smells like oranges.
items.note: Smell like + noun compares an odour to something familiar.

items.pt: cheirar a algo; ter cheiro de
items.example: Her jacket smells of smoke.
items.note: Smell of + noun is another common pattern describing an odour.

items.pt: ter toque de seda; ser macio como seda
items.example: This soft scarf feels like silk.
items.note: Feel like + noun makes a comparison based on touch; different from feel + adjective.

items.example: These biscuits taste like coconut.
items.note: Taste like + noun is a common comparison in the practice exercises.

items.pt: ter gosto de algo; ter sabor de
items.example: This drink tastes of fresh lemons.
items.note: Taste of + noun is an alternative to taste like + noun in the exercise answer key.

items.example: She put a sliced nectarine in her breakfast bowl.
items.note: A smooth-skinned fruit similar to a peach; also labelled in the source illustration.

items.example: The alarm rang when somebody opened the door.
items.note: A warning sound or device; illustrated as a typical comparison for a noise.

items.example: The cake has coconut on top.
items.note: A tropical fruit; its distinctive smell and taste feature in the lesson.

items.example: The dress is made of silk.
items.note: A fine, soft material; used in a comparison about texture.

items.pt: parecer que; dar a impressão visual de que
items.section: C · Impressions: as if, as though, seem and appear
items.example: He looks as if he needs a rest.
items.note: Look as if + clause expresses a visual impression; as though is also possible.

items.pt: parecer que; dar a impressão de que
items.section: C · Impressions: as if, as though, seem and appear
items.example: It looks as though rain is coming.
items.note: Look as though + clause is an alternative to look as if + clause.

items.pt: soar como se; parecer pelo que se ouve que
items.section: C · Impressions: as if, as though, seem and appear
items.example: She sounds as though she has a cold.
items.note: Use sound as though + clause to describe an auditory impression.

items.pt: parecer pelo som que; dar a impressão de que
items.section: C · Impressions: as if, as though, seem and appear
items.example: It sounds as if the meeting has already started.
items.note: An alternative to sound as though + clause.

items.pt: ter a sensação de que; parecer ao toque que
items.section: C · Impressions: as if, as though, seem and appear
items.example: The radiator feels as if it is getting warm.
items.note: Feel as if + clause expresses a physical impression or sensation.

items.pt: ter gosto como se; dar a impressão pelo sabor de que
items.section: C · Impressions: as if, as though, seem and appear
items.example: This soup tastes as if it needs more salt.
items.note: Taste as if + clause makes an inference based on flavour.

items.section: C · Impressions: as if, as though, seem and appear
items.example: Maya seemed happy with her exam results.
items.note: Seem + adjective describes an impression, not a certainty.

items.section: C · Impressions: as if, as though, seem and appear
items.example: He appeared happy when the guests arrived.
items.note: Appear can mean seem; this use is different from become visible.

items.section: C · Impressions: as if, as though, seem and appear
items.example: The library seems to be very busy today.
items.note: Seem + to-infinitive can express an impression about a situation.

items.section: C · Impressions: as if, as though, seem and appear
items.example: The shop appears to be closed.
items.note: Appear to be + adjective or noun describes an impression, not confirmed knowledge.

items.section: C · Impressions: as if, as though, seem and appear
items.example: Taking the earlier train seems like a good idea.
items.note: Before like + noun, seem is the usual choice rather than appear.

items.example: Look at the timetable before we leave.
items.note: Look at means direct your eyes towards something deliberately; see describes perception.

items.example: Look carefully and you will notice the small sign.
items.note: Look describes directing visual attention; carefully says how.

items.example: We watched the children playing in the park.
items.note: Watch often means pay attention over some time, especially when something is moving.

items.example: I rarely watch TV in the morning.
items.note: A common collocation; watch a film on TV is possible.

items.pt: assistir a um filme na televisão
items.example: We watched a film on TV after dinner.
items.note: Watch or see a film on TV are both possible; for cinema attendance, use see a film.

items.word: see a film at the cinema
items.example: We went to see a film at the cinema last night.
items.note: The usual expression for cinema attendance is see a film, not watch a film at the cinema.

items.example: Please listen to the instructions before you start.
items.note: Listen to expresses deliberate attention; hear means receive a sound. Include to before a noun.

items.example: We listen to the radio on long drives.
items.note: A conventional collocation; radio is usually preceded by the.

items.pt: tocar em algo; encostar em algo
items.example: Do not touch the paintings in the gallery.
items.note: Touch means make physical contact, not simply sense a condition.

items.pt: tocar em algo para verificar como está; sentir
items.example: Feel the towel and tell me whether it is dry.
items.note: Feel can mean touch to discover a property, while touch alone emphasises contact.

B: Sense verbs with adjectives and language-help box

units.title: Unit 86 — Uncountable nouns
units.source: Vocabulary study targets from published reference material; Unit 86. Page information, if available, is retained in sourceAudit.
learningObjectives: Recognise common uncountable nouns and use them without an indefinite article or regular plural ending.
Use singular verb agreement with uncountable nouns, including news and homework.
Distinguish experience as knowledge or events and chance as luck or an opportunity.
Use natural unit expressions such as a piece of and a bit of, recognising where piece is not suitable.
Use everyday uncountable nouns including advice, equipment, furniture, progress and scenery.
Distinguish common countable and uncountable travel nouns from the dictionary exercise.

items.example: Could you give me some information about the course?
items.note: Uncountable. Say some information or a piece of information, not an information or informations.

items.example: The homework was difficult but useful.
items.note: Uncountable and used with a singular verb: homework was, not homeworks were.

items.example: Put the rubbish in the bin before you leave.
items.note: Uncountable in this sense. British English for unwanted things to throw away.

items.example: The news is good, and everyone looks relieved.
items.note: Uncountable and singular in grammar, although it ends in -s. Say the news is.

items.example: My manager gave me some useful advice.
items.note: Uncountable. Say some advice or a piece of advice, not advices.

items.example: She saves some of her pocket money every week.
items.note: An uncountable phrase, typically for money parents give children regularly.

items.example: We need better equipment for the camping trip.
items.note: Uncountable. Individual items can be called pieces of equipment, not equipments.

items.example: All the furniture in the living room is new.
items.note: Uncountable. It takes singular agreement: furniture is, not furnitures are.

items.example: We stopped to admire the beautiful mountain scenery.
items.note: Uncountable for the natural surroundings of a place; not sceneries.

items.example: Her knowledge of local history is impressive.
items.note: Uncountable for what someone knows. The usual pattern is knowledge of a subject.

items.example: He has made steady progress with his reading.
items.note: Uncountable. Say progress is, not progresses are in this meaning.

items.example: We made good progress on the project this week.
items.note: Common collocation with uncountable progress; do not use a progress.

items.example: There is not enough room for all the bags in the car.
items.note: Uncountable when it means available space. Room meaning a part of a building is countable.

items.example: Would you like some toast with your eggs?
items.note: Usually uncountable for toasted bread. Say a piece or slice of toast, not a toast in this sense.

items.example: The children's behaviour was excellent during the visit.
items.note: Uncountable in this general sense. British spelling: behaviour; US spelling: behavior.

items.example: There is a bin next to the kitchen door.
items.note: A countable container for rubbish; labelled in the teaching-page illustration.

items.example: We slept in a tent near the lake.
items.note: A countable item of camping equipment shown in the lesson.

items.example: My sleeping bag kept me warm all night.
items.note: A countable piece of camping equipment shown in the illustration.

items.example: Take a torch because the path has no lights.
items.note: British English for a portable electric light; also flashlight in American English.

items.example: She has a lot of experience of working with children.
items.note: Uncountable when it means knowledge or skill gained through doing something.

items.example: He had several amazing experiences while travelling.
items.note: Countable when it means individual things that happen to you. Singular: an experience.

items.example: Winning that game was a matter of chance.
items.note: Uncountable when chance refers to luck or things happening randomly.

items.example: She has had another chance to visit her family abroad.
items.note: Countable when it means an opportunity; plural: chances.

items.pt: ter experiência em algo; ter vivência com algo
items.example: I have some experience of repairing bicycles.
items.note: Uses the uncountable sense of experience; often followed by of + noun or -ing form.

items.example: Give her a chance to explain what happened.
items.note: A countable chance is one opportunity, and can be followed by to + infinitive.

items.section: C · Quantity expressions for uncountable nouns
items.example: My aunt gave me a helpful piece of advice.
items.note: A piece of allows you to count one suggestion, even though advice is uncountable.

items.pt: um equipamento; um item de equipamento
items.section: C · Quantity expressions for uncountable nouns
items.example: This is an important piece of equipment for the laboratory.
items.note: Use a piece of equipment for one item, not an equipment.

items.pt: um móvel; uma peça de mobília
items.section: C · Quantity expressions for uncountable nouns
items.example: We bought a useful piece of furniture for the hallway.
items.note: A piece of furniture means one item, such as a table or a chair.

items.pt: um pedaço de torrada; uma torrada
items.section: C · Quantity expressions for uncountable nouns
items.example: I ate another piece of toast before leaving.
items.note: A common way to count portions of uncountable toast; another slice of toast is also natural.

items.section: C · Quantity expressions for uncountable nouns
items.example: I have an interesting piece of news to tell you.
items.note: An individual item of news; do not say a news.

items.section: C · Quantity expressions for uncountable nouns
items.example: She shared a surprising bit of news with us.
items.note: Informal quantity expression; a piece of news is also possible.

items.section: C · Quantity expressions for uncountable nouns
items.example: There is a bit of rubbish under the table.
items.note: Informal quantity phrase; a piece of rubbish is not the intended pattern in this exercise.

items.pt: um pouco de tarefa de casa
items.section: C · Quantity expressions for uncountable nouns
items.example: I have a bit of homework to finish tonight.
items.note: A bit of measures an amount of uncountable homework.

items.section: C · Quantity expressions for uncountable nouns
items.example: We have made a bit of progress since Monday.
items.note: Use a bit of progress, not a piece of progress, for a small amount of improvement.

items.pt: um pouco de dinheiro de bolso; um pouco da mesada
items.section: C · Quantity expressions for uncountable nouns
items.example: He kept a bit of pocket money for the weekend.
items.note: A bit of expresses a small amount; pocket money is uncountable.

items.section: C · Quantity expressions for uncountable nouns
items.example: We need some information before making a decision.
items.note: Use some with an uncountable noun. Avoid informations and an information.

items.section: C · Quantity expressions for uncountable nouns
items.example: Could I ask you for some advice about the exam?
items.note: Advice is uncountable; some advice is natural even for several suggestions.

items.section: D · Dictionary practice: countable or uncountable
items.example: Public transport is convenient in this city.
items.note: Uncountable in this general sense; dictionary exercise classifies transport as U.

items.section: D · Dictionary practice: countable or uncountable
items.example: Our luggage is still at the hotel.
items.note: Uncountable. Say some luggage, not luggages; suitcase is countable.

items.section: D · Dictionary practice: countable or uncountable
items.example: She packed two suitcases for the trip.
items.note: Countable: a suitcase, two suitcases. Contrasts with luggage.

items.section: D · Dictionary practice: countable or uncountable
items.example: We ate some pasta with tomatoes.
items.note: Generally uncountable as a food; dictionary exercise classifies it as U.

items.section: D · Dictionary practice: countable or uncountable
items.example: The traffic is heavy near the station this morning.
items.note: Uncountable; takes a singular verb. Traffic refers to vehicles moving on roads.

items.section: D · Dictionary practice: countable or uncountable
items.example: There was an accident on the motorway yesterday.
items.note: Countable: an accident, several accidents. Contrasts with uncountable traffic.

items.section: D · Dictionary practice: countable or uncountable
items.example: We need more space for another desk.
items.note: An uncountable synonym of room when referring to available space; used in the practice answer key.
